text: The Virgin of the Rocks (Italian: Vergine delle rocce), also known as the Madonna of the Rocks, refers to two paintings by the Italian Renaissance artist Leonardo da Vinci, depicting the same subject— the adoration of the Christ child by the infant John the Baptist— with nearly identical compositions but significant differences in detail. The earlier version, generally considered the prime work, is unrestored and hangs in the Louvre Museum in Paris, while the other, restored between 2008 and 2010, is located in the National Gallery, London. Both paintings are approximately 2 metres (over 6 feet) high, painted in oils on wooden panels, though the Louvre version has been transferred to canvas. The scenes feature the Virgin Mary, the Christ child, the infant John the Baptist, and the angel Uriel, arranged in a triangular composition against a rocky background, which gives the paintings their name. The main compositional differences include the angel’s gaze and right hand: in the Louvre version, the angel’s hand is raised with the index finger pointing at John and his eyes are directed toward the viewer, whereas in the London version, the hand rests on the knee and the eyes are turned downward. The London painting has sharper contrasts, more defined forms, and brighter lighting, while the Louvre version features softer, more hazy forms and a warmer, subtler lighting effect, enhanced by sfumato. The Louvre painting is about 8 cm (3 inches) taller than the London version and is dated to around 1483–1486, with most art historians agreeing it was entirely painted by Leonardo. The London version is ascribed to Leonardo with a date before 1508, and although initially thought to be partially completed by his assistants, a 2008–2010 restoration concluded that the majority of the work is by Leonardo, though debate persists, especially regarding the flowers and other details. Both paintings were created for the chapel of the Confraternity of the Immaculate Conception in Milan’s San Francesco Maggiore church, commissioned in 1483, with a due date of December 8, 1483. The contract specified a central panel showing the Virgin Mary, Christ child, and two prophets with angels, along with side panels featuring musical and singing angels. The central panel was to be completed by Leonardo and the de Predis brothers, with the final payment due upon delivery. The altarpiece was delivered on August 18, 1508, and Ambrogio received two payments totaling 200 Lire in 1507 and 1508. The London version was sold by the church in 1785 to Gavin Hamilton, who brought it to England, and it was later acquired by the National Gallery in 1880 for 9,000 guineas, though it was reported to be in poor condition and sometimes attributed to Bernardino Luini. In 2005, an infra-red reflectogram revealed a pentimento showing a woman kneeling with her hand outstretched, suggesting an original intention to depict an adoration of the infant Jesus, and in 2021, an AI company reconstructed this using Leonardo’s oeuvre. The two angel panels, now in the National Gallery, were completed between 1490 and 1495; the red angel is attributed to Ambrogio de Predis and the green one to an unknown assistant, possibly Francesco Napoletano. These panels were originally intended to flank the central panel but may have been placed higher on the altarpiece. The relationship between the two paintings remains debated, with most authorities agreeing that the Louvre version is earlier and the London version is a later derivative, fulfilling the original commission. The subject, rooted in a non-Biblical tradition involving John the Baptist’s journey to Egypt with the Archangel Uriel, was common in Renaissance Florence, with artists like Fra Filippo Lippi, Raphael, and Michelangelo depicting similar scenes. The Louvre painting is considered a perfect example of Leonardo’s sfumato technique and has not undergone significant restoration, preserving its original appearance under thick yellow varnish, while the London version has undergone cleaning and conservation in 2009–2010. The London painting lacks haloes and John’s traditional staff, and its floral details are fanciful, whereas the Louvre version features botanically accurate flowers. The two paintings were briefly exhibited together in 2011–2012, and the Louvre version is widely regarded as stylistically closer to Leonardo’s early works, while the London version reflects a more mature style.

The relationship between the two Virgin of the Rocks paintings—those in the Louvre and London—remains much debated, with discussions focusing on their dates, authorship, and symbolism. It is generally accepted by art historians that the Louvre version is the earlier work, stylistically closer to Leonardo's earlier period, while the London version reflects a more mature style and is thus considered later and derivative. Martin Davies, former director of the National Gallery, and Kenneth Clark agree that the Louvre painting was created prior to 1481, with the London version dating from 1483, fulfilling the original 1483 commission. However, some scholars, including Davies, argue that 1483 is too late for the Louvre painting and suggest it may have been begun and completed in Florence before the commission. Wasserman, Ottino della Chiesa, and others note that the measurements of both paintings fit the altarpiece, making it unlikely that Leonardo painted a work of that size before the commission, and propose that the Louvre painting was extended to fit the arched shape, with the joint no longer visible due to a 19th-century transfer to canvas. Davies and Clark suggest Leonardo painted the London version in the 1480s to fulfill the commission, based on the earlier Louvre work. The most widely accepted theory is that Leonardo painted the Louvre Virgin of the Rocks to fulfill the 1483 commission, then sold it to another client, and painted the London version as a replacement, with the Louvre painting sold in the late 1480s after payment disputes, the London version begun around 1486 as a substitute, and not ready for installation until 1508. This theory, attributed to Venturi and Poggi and supported by the National Gallery and Louvre websites, is also endorsed by Martin Kemp, who dates the Louvre painting to 1483–1490 and the London version to 1495–1508. However, Taylor argues that the London painting is stylistically earlier, more meticulous, and consistent with Leonardo's Florentine training, while the Louvre version shares features with the Last Supper and Virgin and Child with St Anne, suggesting a later date in the 1490s and a different clientele. It is universally agreed that the Louvre Virgin of the Rocks is entirely by Leonardo da Vinci, while the London version is generally seen as designed by Leonardo and executed by his assistants. The Louvre website and various authors suggest the entire London painting was by Ambrogio de Predis, under Leonardo’s supervision between 1485 and 1508, or largely by de Predis with minor input from Leonardo. Since recent cleaning, National Gallery curator Luke Syson has stated that the revealed quality indicates the work is mostly by Leonardo, with workshop involvement less than previously thought. Geologist Ann C. Pizzorusso claims geological inaccuracies in the London version, unlike the Louvre version, suggesting it is unlikely to be by Leonardo, but Taylor disputes this, noting Pizzorusso had not seen the glacial lakes and misidentified moss as sandstone boulders. One of the earliest known direct copies of the Louvre version is the Paliotto leonardesco (ca 1487–90) in the Museo Baroffio, and another painting (ca 1494–98) in the Cheramy Collection, believed by Carlo Pedretti to be by Leonardo himself. Angela Ottino della Chiesa identifies four paintings derived from The Virgin of the Rocks: the Holy Family and St. John by Bernardino Luini in Madrid, the Thuelin Madonna by Marco d'Oggiono in Paris, and the Holy Infants Embracing by Joos van Cleve in Naples. The image was widely copied by Flemish artists, including Joos van Cleve and Quentin Matsys, with a small painting in Chatsworth attributed to Matsys and a smaller oil on wood copy in a private Berlin collection possibly by Joos van Cleve or his circle. A 16th-century copy is held in the Royal Collection and was given to Queen Victoria in 1847 by her husband, Prince Albert.
